leaders.priorInstitution: Little Rock, Arkansas public schools (previously Mattoon, Illinois public schools)
leaders.notes: Hired as acting president of the newly opened Arkansas Industrial University because the trustees could not secure a permanent leader; he organized the institution, managed its business affairs, hired faculty and taught courses. The university awarded him an honorary Master of Arts degree in 1880.

leaders.priorInstitution: Arkansas Industrial University (same institution, internal appointment)
leaders.notes: A Yale graduate (1853) and former Union Army captain who had been the university's treasurer since its 1871 founding; Old Main opened during his presidency. He left when appointed state adjutant general and ran unsuccessfully for governor in 1875.

leaders.priorInstitution: Arkansas Industrial University (same institution, internal appointment)
leaders.notes: Second, non-acting term leading the university, returning to the presidency from the normal department after Albert Bishop's departure. He later became superintendent of the Fort Smith school district (1884) and of Fayetteville public schools (1889).

leaders.priorInstitution: North Carolina Military Institute
leaders.nextRoleInstitution: Georgia Agricultural and Mechanical College at Milledgeville
leaders.notes: West Point graduate (1842) and Confederate lieutenant general who had chaired mathematics at Washington College and Davidson College before running the North Carolina Military Institute. His administration raised academic standards and grew enrollment; he resigned in 1884 for health reasons.

leaders.priorInstitution: Oakland College, Mississippi
leaders.notes: Virginia-born former Confederate officer whose administration emphasized institutional regulation, holding forty-two faculty meetings before Christmas of his first college year. He resigned in 1887 in opposition to a General Assembly reorganization of the university.

leaders.priorTitle: Chair of Mathematics and Logic (then acting president)
leaders.priorInstitution: Arkansas Industrial University (same institution, internal appointment)
leaders.nextRoleInstitution: Alabama Central College, later Brenau College, Gainesville, Georgia
leaders.notes: Promoted from the mathematics and logic chair (1885-1887) to acting president and then confirmed as the university's fifth president. Student attendance rose to roughly 700 during his tenure, which a faculty report called a period of progress unprecedented in the institution's history.

leaders.priorTitle: Superintendent of Public Instruction of Virginia (and ex officio member of the University of Virginia board)
leaders.priorInstitution: Commonwealth of Virginia
leaders.notes: A former president of Virginia Agricultural and Mechanical College, he changed the institution's name from Arkansas Industrial University to University of Arkansas in 1899 and created independent departments of history, civil engineering and electrical engineering. He retired in 1902 for health reasons and returned to Virginia.

leaders.priorInstitution: Clemson Agricultural College, South Carolina
leaders.notes: A Baptist minister and educator, he was the first University of Arkansas president born after the Civil War and the youngest person to hold the office. He secured funding for several campus buildings still in use, and later entered educational publishing in St. Louis.

leaders.priorTitle: President of the alumni association and member of the Board of Trustees (previously prosecuting attorney and circuit judge, 4th Judicial District of Arkansas)
leaders.priorInstitution: University of Arkansas (same institution, internal appointment)
leaders.nextRole: Member of the U.S. House of Representatives
leaders.notes: A lawyer admitted to the Arkansas bar in 1883, he came to the presidency from the university's own alumni association leadership and board of trustees. He resigned at the end of the 1911-1912 school year and was elected to Congress two years later, serving seven terms.

leaders.priorTitle: Chair of History and Political Science
leaders.priorInstitution: University of Arkansas (same institution, internal appointment)
leaders.notes: Acting president who reorganized the teaching departments into three colleges (Agriculture, Arts and Sciences, and Engineering) and created a publicity committee that became the university relations office. Despite campus support, the Board of Trustees passed him over for the permanent post.

leaders.priorTitle: Chair of the Mathematics Department (and acting president)
leaders.priorInstitution: University of Arkansas (same institution, internal appointment)
leaders.notes: Longest-serving president in the institution's history; enrollment nearly quadrupled and major campus buildings were constructed during his 26 years. He died in office in a traffic accident near West Fork, Arkansas, on September 12, 1939, while returning from business in Little Rock.

leaders.priorInstitution: University of Arkansas School of Law (same institution, internal appointment)
leaders.nextRole: Member of the U.S. House of Representatives, then U.S. Senator
leaders.notes: Elevated from the law faculty (which he joined in 1936) to the presidency at age 34. His presidency was terminated by trustees newly appointed by Governor Homer Adkins, whom Fulbright's mother Roberta, editor of the Northwest Arkansas Times, had opposed; he went on to the U.S. House in 1942, the Senate in 1944, and a long chairmanship of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.

leaders.priorTitle: Registrar and Director of General Extension
leaders.priorInstitution: University of Arkansas (same institution, internal appointment)
leaders.notes: The first Arkansas-born president of the university, promoted after serving as registrar since 1916 and extension director since 1919. He mobilized the campus for World War II, saying the University of Arkansas enlisted for the duration when Pearl Harbor was bombed; he resigned in 1946, served into early 1947, and died in Fayetteville that December.

leaders.priorInstitution: Bennington College, Vermont
leaders.notes: An economist recruited from Bennington College who oversaw the racial integration of the university, when Silas H. Hunt enrolled in the School of Law, along with creation of the Fine Arts Center and the Medical Center at Little Rock. He left in 1951 for the Rutgers presidency and later led the National Conference of Christians and Jews.

leaders.priorInstitution: Alabama College
leaders.notes: Held a Princeton doctorate and served in the Navy in World War II; at Arkansas he won North Central Association accreditation of doctoral programs, launched the university's first major research push and established a School of Nursing at Fayetteville and the Little Rock Medical Center. He resigned in 1959 for the North Carolina State chancellorship.

leaders.priorInstitution: University of Arkansas (same institution, internal appointment)
leaders.nextRole: Vice President for Health Sciences (head of the Medical Center)
leaders.notes: Acting president named when John Tyler Caldwell resigned, having joined the university in 1954 as an assistant to the president for public relations. When Mullins was appointed president in 1960 he became vice president for health sciences, later leaving in 1970 for the National Institutes of Health.

leaders.priorInstitution: Auburn University, Alabama
leaders.notes: Came to the presidency after eleven years (1949-1960) as vice president of Auburn University. He retired in 1974; the university's main research library is named in his honor, and he received honorary degrees from Hendrix College (1965) and the University of Arkansas (1987).

leaders.priorInstitution: University of Maryland
leaders.notes: An agricultural economist with two decades at North Carolina State before four years as chancellor of the University of Maryland. He built the administrative architecture of what became the University of Arkansas System, creating an executive cabinet and appointing chancellors at the regional campuses, and oversaw construction of Kimpel Hall and a new business building.

leaders.priorTitle: Vice President for the Division of Agriculture
leaders.priorInstitution: University of Arkansas (same institution, internal appointment)
leaders.notes: Promoted from within after joining the University of Arkansas in 1975 as vice president for agriculture. As president he created the chancellor's position at the Fayetteville campus, founded the University of Arkansas Press, and built the Center for Continuing Education; he left in 1984 to become president of his alma mater Auburn University, retiring there in 1992.

leaders.priorInstitution: Arkansas State University, Jonesboro (a different Arkansas public system, not the UA System)
leaders.nextRole: Member of the U.S. House of Representatives, then Associate Justice of the Arkansas Supreme Court
leaders.nextRoleInstitution: United States Congress, then Arkansas Supreme Court
leaders.notes: A former Arkansas attorney general and congressman from the 4th District who came to the UA System presidency directly from three years as president of Arkansas State University in Jonesboro; he moved the president's office to Little Rock. He returned to politics for three more congressional terms, was elected to the Arkansas Supreme Court in 1996 and retired in 2004.

leaders.priorTitle: President of Corpus Christi State University (Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi); earlier chancellor of the three-campus South Texas University System
leaders.priorInstitution: Corpus Christi State University / Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi, Texas
leaders.notes: A UA-Fayetteville alumnus who returned to his alma mater in 1990 after roughly 22 years in Texas higher education, including about 13 years leading the Corpus Christi institution. Enrollment in the UA System grew from about 30,000 students on five campuses to nearly 70,000 across 17 campuses and units, with roughly $2 billion in construction and renovation.

leaders.priorTitle: Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs
leaders.priorInstitution: University of Texas at Arlington
leaders.notes: A chemist and former dean of the J. William Fulbright College of Arts and Sciences at UA-Fayetteville (2003) who returned from UT Arlington to begin as system president on November 1, 2011. He founded eVersity, the state's first fully online institution, in 2015, added UA-Pulaski Technical College and UA-Rich Mountain (2016) and East Arkansas Community College (2024), and announced his retirement on July 16, 2024, effective January 15, 2025.

leaders.priorTitle: Associate Vice President of Texas A&M University and Executive Director of the Bush School of Government & Public Service in Washington, D.C.
leaders.priorInstitution: Texas A&M University
leaders.notes: Retired U.S. Air Force lieutenant general and former superintendent of the U.S. Air Force Academy, unanimously approved by the University of Arkansas Board of Trustees on November 18, 2024 and started January 15, 2025. The search that produced him was run for the UA Foundation Board by Greenwood Asher & Associates (Julie Holley and Marion Frenche), with trustee Scott Ford leading; seven candidates formally applied. He remains in office, so the Greenwood Asher engagement is closed and there is no active UA System presidential search.

leaders.priorInstitution: Arkansas State University, Jonesboro (same institution, internal continuation; he had led ASU since July 1, 1995, before the 2006 system reorganization)
leaders.nextRole: Consultant to Academic Partnerships, LLC and president and chairman of the American University System, while holding a distance-education faculty assignment at Arkansas State University
leaders.nextRoleInstitution: Academic Partnerships, LLC / Arkansas State University
leaders.notes: First president of the ASU System. Formally titled James Leslie Wyatt, he became ASU president on July 1, 1995 and in October 2006 the Board of Trustees created a separate system office, with Wyatt remaining as system president and Robert L. Potts named the first chancellor of the Jonesboro campus. He announced his resignation at the May 2010 quarterly board meeting, effective June 30, 2010, and was unanimously designated President Emeritus.

leaders.priorInstitution: Arkansas State University, Jonesboro (same system, internal appointment)
leaders.notes: Asked by the Board of Trustees to serve as interim system president from July 1, 2010 while a permanent successor to Les Wyatt was recruited; Dan Howard became interim Jonesboro chancellor on his recommendation. Potts had been president of the University of North Alabama (1990-2004), general counsel of the University of Alabama System, and chancellor of the North Dakota University System before becoming ASU-Jonesboro's first chancellor in fall 2006. He retired to Florence, Alabama in 2011 and died October 28, 2022.

leaders.priorInstitution: Henderson State University, Arkadelphia, Arkansas (a separate Arkansas public university, not in the ASU System)
leaders.nextRoleInstitution: American Association of State Colleges and Universities (AASCU)
leaders.notes: Second president of the ASU System, known publicly as Chuck Welch. Named by the Board of Trustees in November 2010 and formally beginning in April 2011, he became the longest-tenured higher education president or chancellor in Arkansas over nearly 13 years. Earlier ASU System and Arkansas roles included chancellor of UA Community College at Hope-Texarkana and vice chancellor for academic affairs at ASU-Beebe. He resigned in November 2023, was designated President Emeritus in December 2023, and became AASCU's seventh president and CEO on January 15, 2024; the ASU System's own timeline lists his tenure as 2011-2023.

leaders.priorTitle: Chancellor Emeritus (retired Chancellor of Arkansas State University-Mountain Home)
leaders.priorInstitution: Arkansas State University-Mountain Home (same system, internal appointment)
leaders.nextRole: Returned to retirement, continuing as an ASU System consultant on the CREST Center project before a second interim presidency in December 2025
leaders.notes: First of two interim presidencies. Announced December 8, 2023 and effective January 15, 2024, he was chosen for his familiarity with the system and its leadership; the board stated he would not be a candidate for the permanent job. He had retired in July 2023 after 11 years as chancellor of ASU-Mountain Home and was designated Chancellor Emeritus on July 18, 2023. He served until Brendan Kelly took office on September 23, 2024.

leaders.priorInstitution: University of West Georgia, Carrollton, Georgia
leaders.notes: Third president of the ASU System, selected by the Board of Trustees on June 5, 2024 and beginning September 23, 2024. He came from the University of West Georgia presidency, which he had held since 2020, after earlier service as chancellor of USC Upstate, interim president of the University of South Carolina, and vice president for advancement at the University of West Florida. He announced his departure on December 10, 2025 to become president of his alma mater Eastern Michigan University, starting there April 1, 2026.

leaders.priorTitle: Chancellor Emeritus of Arkansas State University-Mountain Home and ASU System consultant; previously interim ASU System president in 2024
leaders.priorInstitution: Arkansas State University System (same system, internal appointment)
leaders.notes: Second interim presidency. The Board of Trustees named him interim system president on December 12, 2025, effective immediately, on contract terms consistent with his previous interim service and without scheduling a permanent search at that meeting. He served until Todd Shields took office July 1, 2026, and recommended A-State provost Calvin White Jr. as interim Jonesboro chancellor.

leaders.priorInstitution: Arkansas State University, Jonesboro (same system, internal promotion; he was chancellor from August 15, 2022 to June 30, 2026)
leaders.notes: Fourth president of the ASU System, appointed by unanimous vote of the Board of Trustees at a special called meeting on May 26, 2026, effective July 1, 2026, succeeding Brendan Kelly (with Robin Myers serving as interim in between). A political scientist with a Ph.D. from the University of Kentucky, he was dean of the J. William Fulbright College of Arts and Sciences at the University of Arkansas from 2014 before being named A-State's chancellor on July 11, 2022, where he oversaw an enrollment increase of nearly 30 percent as the fourth appointed chancellor and 14th person to lead the Jonesboro campus.
